content: Sickle cell disease is a group of genetic disorders defined by the presence of at least one hemoglobin S (Hb S) allele and a second abnormal allele. This combination can lead to abnormal hemoglobin polymerization, resulting in a symptomatic disorder. Since sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive condition, it is a suitable candidate for gene therapy. This is because introducing a single normal copy of the defective gene into diseased cells can restore a normal phenotype. The purpose of this review was to evaluate whether gene therapy can improve survival and prevent symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. Additionally, the review aimed to assess the risks of gene therapy in comparison to its potential long-term benefits for individuals with this condition. To gather relevant data, the researchers searched the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register. This register includes references obtained from extensive electronic database searches, as well as from relevant journals and conference proceedings. Online trial registries were also searched. The most recent search of the Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register was conducted on September 21, 2020. The review included all randomized or quasi-randomized clinical trials, including phase 1, 2, or 3 trials, that investigated gene therapy for individuals with sickle cell disease, regardless of their age or clinical setting. However, no clinical trials of gene therapy for sickle cell disease were identified. As a result, no data were available for analysis, and no conclusions could be drawn regarding the efficacy or safety of gene therapy for this condition. The authors concluded that there are no randomized or quasi-randomized clinical trials available to provide evidence on the use of gene therapy for sickle cell disease. Consequently, no objective recommendations can be made for its use in clinical practice. This review highlights the urgent need for well-designed, randomized controlled trials to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of gene therapy for sickle cell disease.
